#6459. Progressives and moderates rejoice: 6 takeaways from the midterms

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses an election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday after Democrats were projected to win the House. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats were savoring their midterm election rout Wednesday after decisively flipping both the House and Senate.

“Last night was beyond even our largest expectations of what could happen,” Arizona Rep. Greg Stanton said on a press call.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat in line to become the first Black speaker, predicted Democrats would hold at least 255 seats next year, which would be the largest majority for either party since Democrats won 257 seats in 2008.

In the Senate, the Democratic Caucus was poised to hold at least 54 seats after seismic red-state gains, with two key races too close to call.

“What we have now seen is a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now but on into the future,” Charles E. Schumer, the chamber’s top Democrat, said Wednesday.

Here are six takeaways from the midterm elections:

Democratic gains were so sweeping that both ideological wings of the party had plenty to celebrate. The moderate Blue Dogs more than doubled their current membership, with at least 22 Blue Dog PAC-endorsed candidates winning Tuesday. Meanwhile, the Congressional Progressive Caucus anticipated at least 25 new members.

For House progressives, swing-seat wins in Michigan and California were signs that their candidates’ message resonated in battleground races and that Democrats should move to implement those progressive ideas next year.

“Big majorities can get big things done,” Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar said on a Wednesday press call.

Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider, the chair of the center-left New Democrat Coalition, told reporters he had a strong relationship with Casar and envisioned different factions of the party working together.

“It doesn’t matter what you call your idea. If your idea is going to help us move the ball forward, join us at the table,” Schneider said.

Army veteran Cait Conley, who was leading GOP Rep. Mike Lawler in a race that remained uncalled Wednesday afternoon, said she’d been open about having differences with incoming New York Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. But she said Democrats across the political spectrum needed to prioritize “real solutions for the American people.”

“If we don’t make that our priority, if we don’t show that that is more important than anything else … then I think the voters are going to show us in 2028 that they’re not going to accept that,” she said on the New Dems press call.

While the president cast a shadow over the entire midterm map, three of his marquee candidates were among the night’s biggest busts.

Trump was behind appointed South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham every step of the way, helping her win a contested primary to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, on the ballot. But Graham lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in a stunning upset. In North Carolina, Trump had publicly urged Michael Whatley to run for the state’s open seat. But the former Republican National Committee chairman lost to Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper by 20 points. And most significantly, in Texas, Trump elevated scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton over Republican incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. But the president’s support wasn’t enough to stave off a general election drubbing at the hands of Democrat James Talarico.

Even Rep. Julia Letlow, Trump’s pick for Senate in deep-red Louisiana, won her election by less than 2 points.

Republicans in seven states successfully embarked on a mid-decade redistricting spree aimed at boosting GOP candidates. But the push couldn’t overcome the political headwinds that battered the Republican brand. In California, where Democrats launched a redistricting push in response to the Texas redraw, the new map proved more beneficial: Democrats are poised to flip at least four seats they redrew in their favor.

Republican Alex Mealer was the heavy favorite to win a redrawn Houston-area seat that Trump would have carried by 20 points. She raised $2.8 million to first-time Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez’ $215,000. Yet Gutierrez won the contest by double digits. In an interview on MS NOW, Gutierrez said her campaign proved that “you don’t need money to buy a congressional race.” She wasn’t the only under-the-radar House contender to pull off an unexpected victory Tuesday. In North Carolina, several low-profile and under-funded Democrats appear poised to pull off unlikely upsets, though the races remain too close to call.

Democrats have chased the dream of a blue Texas for more than 30 years — and always came up short. Until Tuesday. The party notched a series of stunning wins in the nation’s most consequential red state — from Talarico’s decisive victory in the Senate contest to winning several key House races to capturing the governor’s mansion. Democrats seized every elected statewide position on the ballot and flipped the state House, according to The Associated Press. “They said it could not be done,’’ Democratic Rep. Christian Menefee told supporters Tuesday night. “We did it.”

Democrats made deep gains in red states and districts across the country, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, while races in Alaska and Mississippi remained too close to call. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called it “probably the political worst case scenario for a midterm election.”

But Democrats didn’t appear convinced that their brand had completely rebounded from deep losses two years ago, saying they had work to do over the next two years.

“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday, of course, are still skeptical,” Schumer said.

Similarly, Casar and Rep. Pramila Jayapal both warned Democrats not to assume that Tuesday’s wins had resolved the party’s branding issues.

“We still are not particularly popular as a Democratic Party across the country,” Jayapal told reporters. “I think we’ve got a shot to show that we can deliver on the kind of bold populist change that people ran on and won on.”

#6458. The Best Frozen Lasagna, According to Our Taste Test

Frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →

Big Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

Why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

We cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

#6457. The Absolute Best Pie Recipes, According to Eater Staff

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

#6455. Astrophysicists Cross Another Dark Matter Candidate Off Their List: Stupendously Large Black Holes

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.

There are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe. They're hypothetical too, but are massive objects, so their presence should be detectable in a way that particles aren't.

All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different. But PBHs have fairly well-defined search strategies that should detect them if they exist. If they exist, then cosmologists should find evidence of them in the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

The CMB is relic radiation from the Big Bang itself, the oldest detectable light that exists. It was released when the Universe was only about 380,000 years old. For the most part, the CMB appears smooth and uniform, or isotropic. But increasingly powerful detectors let cosmologists examine the CMB for minor fluctuations. Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. Yes, that's two billions one after another.

This is a temperature map of the CMB created with data from the ESA's Planck spacecraft. The CMB can only be measured from space, and Planck's job was to measure anisotropies in the CMB. The different colours show temperature differences, and those differences correspond to where the first galaxies formed. Image Credit: NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=130789180

New research published in Physical Review Letters says that SLABs can't be dark matter. It's titled "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," and the lead author is Christopher Gerlach. Gerlach is a theoretical physicist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and its PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence.

âA possible solution to the puzzle of dark matter was that it might have collected shortly after the Big Bang in giant black holes with masses ranging from 100 million to 10 billion billion times that of the sun," said lead author Gerlatz.

This work is largely based on the ESA's Planck satellite. The Planck satellite ended its mission in 2013, but researchers are still generating new insights from its data. Part of that is because of more raw computing power. But it's also because they can cross-correlate it with new data from sources that didn't exist back in 2013. Physicists also have better ways to filter out interference, like that from the Milky Way.

âThat we are still generating new insights into the universeâs evolution and structure 13 years after it was shut down only emphasizes how important the Planck satellite was and is to physicists," explained Gerlach.

âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â - Nicholas Leister, Johannes Gutenberg University.

SLABs, if they're real, formed from overdensities of matter after the Big Bang. They didn't need to form massive stars, burn their fuel, and explode as supernovae. They skipped that step, and are too massive for that, anyway. Since they're theorized to have formed so early, before massive objects like galaxy clusters, they should be the only things that left such an imprint on the CMB.

âIf these SLABs had existed in large numbers and contained significant amounts of dark matter, they would have left a characteristic imprint on the CMB through their unique perturbations, or, in a word, making it grainy," said study co-author Nicholas Leister, also a JGU physicist.

This image is an artist's interpretation of what primordial black holes could look like. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these. Image Credit: NASA

Previous work has all but eliminated the possibility that regular primordial black holes could account for all dark matter. But what about SLABs? Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins?

To find out, the researchers first modelled SLABs and how they would affect the CMB. Then they compared the modelled effects to the actual CMB. The result was clear: the CMB doesn't have the characteristic graininess that SLABs should have imprinted on it.

"In this work, we have shown that the production of stupendously large PBHs would generate large DM isocurvature perturbations, tightly constrained by CMB and BAO data," the authors explain.

"We show that primordial black holes (PBHs) in the Stupendously Large Black Hole mass range (Mâ³1011Mâ) produce isocurvature perturbations exceeding current Planck Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) limits, thereby excluding them as a significant dark matter component," the authors conclude.

This artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disc. SMBH are massive and they're real. But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. Credit: ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser

The results also counter some other thinking regarding PBHs and dark matter. When the JWST discovered its notorious early massive galaxies, galaxies so massive that they challenged models of galaxy formation, it set the astrophysical community in motion searching for explanations. Astrophysicists cast their net wide, and one explanation they caught concerned PBHs. One 2022 study, titled "Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.

But that's unlikely to be true, according to these results.

"They also challenge scenarios attributing the early massive galaxy candidates observed by James Webb Space Telescope to PBH-induced fluctuations," the researchers write.

SLABs were also potential explanations for another unexplained phenomenon. A gravitational wave background hum pervades the Universe, sensed by Pulsar Timing Arrays, and some researchers asked if SLABs could be responsible. "These questions are also unlikely to be answered by SLABs, since our findings show that they didnât exist in large numbers," said Nicholas Leister. âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â

So the search for dark matter candidates continues. It's possible that no one type of object or particle makes up dark matter. Dark matter may be a collective effect generated by different particles, objects, or phenomena.

But it looks like SLABs are no longer in contention.

#6453. How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit Manager of Audience Strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed 2-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

After years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit Senior Test Kitchen Editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in new equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, Director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in New Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hard-working, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”

A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

Most importantly, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6452. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

#6451. When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

The study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:

Isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

One issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser shows how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Said Eser:

We are not claiming to have discovered a new gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

Further Reading: Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6449. These former members are returning to Congress next year

Former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, here at a Oct. 20 campaign event near Ohio University in Athens, won his comeback bid Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.

The winners included alumni who dusted themselves off after election losses just two years ago. But other winners haven’t been in office in nearly two decades, their service predating the addition of a women’s restroom in the House (more recent than you may guess).

Here’s how these former members did on election night:

Carl lost a primary to fellow Republican Rep. Barry Moore in 2024 after a new map placed them in the same district. But with Moore running for the Senate in 2026, Carl had an easier path back to his old seat, which was redrawn again this year. He defeated his Democratic opponent Tuesday by 18 points.

It has been nearly two decades since Solis last served in Congress. She left in 2009 to serve as President Barack Obama’s first Labor secretary. Solis was in her sixth term as a Los Angeles county supervisor when she announced a bid for Congress after California voters approved a map that created five Democratic pickup opportunities.

Solis faced limited resistance on her path to victory in the 38th District, especially after Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez opted to run for the redrawn 41st District.

Bean is making her way back to the House after losing her suburban Chicagoland seat in the conservative tea party wave of 2010.

A decade-and-a-half later, she won an eight-way primary for the 8th District seat Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi vacated for an unsuccessful Senate bid. Winning the nomination all but guaranteed Bean a November victory in the deep-blue seat.

One of the cycle’s biggest comeback stories was in the Buckeye State, where Sherrod Brown was mounting a bid two years after Republican Bernie Moreno had unseated him. Positioning himself as an opponent of data centers, Brown defeated appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the remainder of now Vice President JD Vance’s term. He could take office as early as December but would have to run again in 2028 if he wants another full term.

First elected in 2018, Allred left Congress two years ago after an unsuccessful Senate campaign against Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. After briefly launching a second Senate bid, Allred switched to a redrawn open House seat and won his primary over Rep. Julie Elizabeth Johnson, his successor in the chamber. Allred had no trouble winning his general election Tuesday for a fourth House term.

McAdams served one term in Congress representing a battleground Utah seat, before being unseated by Republican Burgess Owens in 2020. But after a state judge approved a new congressional map that created a heavily Democratic seat anchored in Salt Lake City, McAdams jumped into the race. He comfortably won his primary over more progressive opponents and stomped his way to a second term on Tuesday.

Once a high-ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, Luria lost her Hampton Roads seat in 2022 to Republican Jen Kiggans.

But a week after Virginia Democrats posted strong showings in the commonwealth’s 2025 off-year elections, Luria launched her House comeback bid and went on to oust Kiggans on Tuesday.

Former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers left the House after the 2014 elections and made his first Senate bid 10 years later. He lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin but sought the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters the following year.

Rogers tried to take advantage of Democratic divisions between primary winner Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, even winning a late endorsement from the congresswoman. But it was not enough to stop El-Sayed on Tuesday.

Republican John E. Sununu served three terms in the House and one in the Senate before losing to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. With Shaheen retiring, Sununu attempted a comeback but ended up losing decisively to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

Perriello won an upset victory in a Charlottesville-anchored district in 2008 before losing reelection in the tea party wave two years later. He launched a comeback bid this cycle for the current version of the seat, but the Republican incumbent, John McGuire, narrowly prevailed.

Two years after losing her at-large House seat to Republican Nick Begich, Peltola chose to challenge Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The race was rocked by late revelations by The New York Times that top aides to Peltola’s campaign were closely involved in recruiting a second candidate named Dan Sullivan into the race to peel votes from the incumbent. As of Wednesday afternoon, Peltola was clinging to a narrow lead as votes were counted.

#6448. Baby, She's Back! SpaceX Catches a Starship From Orbit for First Time

SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. The arm-capture system, nicknamed "Mechazilla," had been used three times previously to capture Starship Super Heavy boosters during suborbital flight tests, but this was the first time for a second stage coming in hot from orbit.

"Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot said.

In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September.

Years of development â including 15 full-scale flight tests since 2023 â led up to today's orbital catch, which Huot called "the Holy Grail of spaceflight." The achievement took the sting out of the previous day's aborted effort to catch the rocket's booster using the same system, minutes after liftoff. SpaceX said the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. The root cause of the alarm is under investigation.

SpaceX plans to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.

This 15th flight test proceeded almost in textbook fashion, aside from the boosterâs offshore splashdown on launch day. During the first hours of its 14-orbit flight, Starship deployed 26 more next-generation satellites for SpaceXâs Starlink broadband internet network. All of the satellites were in good health and beginning to raise their orbits to operational altitude, the company said.

At the end of the trip, the second stage fired a single engine for roughly 10 seconds to start its descent through the atmosphere. As the temperatures rose, a brlght glow surrounded Ship 42âs leading edges. The craft executed a bellyflop maneuver to maximize its deceleration. Then it righted itself, and fired its engines a final time to sink into Mechazillaâs arms.

SpaceX employees around the country and hundreds of onlookers near the Texas launch site cheered, while âBaby, Come Backâ played on the soundtrack for the webcast. âBaby, sheâs back,â Huot joked.

Bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system are scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA's Artemis III mission.

In a post to X, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team on today's successful catch. "It was almost magic ... Making more believers by the day," he wrote. Using emojis, Isaacman said the achievement brought the United States "one step closer" to putting an American flag once more on the moon.

SpaceX's team will analyze the data gathered about Starship's performance, including the ability of Ship 42's heat shield to stand up to the rigors of atmospheric re-entry. The company is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana.

In the long term, Musk envisions creating a fleet of Starships that could offer point-to-point rocket travel on Earth, as well as mass transit to Mars and other off-Earth destinations. Cryptocurrency investor Chun Wang has already announced his intention to take Starship trips around the moon and Mars.

"I donât think you guys understand," a software engineer named Will DePue wrote in a post to X. "You will get the chance to go to space in your lifetime. New era."

Science journalist Alan Boyle is the creator of Cosmic Log, a veteran of MSNBC.com and NBC News Digital, and the author of "The Case for Pluto." He's based in the Seattle area, but the cosmos is his home.
