#6411. Fermi’s 14-Year All-Sky Map Bridges Astronomy’s Elusive "MeV Gap"

Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. Weâve always had trouble measuring them in the âmega-electron voltâ (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the âMeV gapâ. But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration recently published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20-200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray observatory, that can capture radiation at the x-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher end ones.

But why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit rather than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

At high energies - around 1 giga-electron volt (GeV), the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, at the lower 20-200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from. Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide - more than forty times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the Sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

However, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data thereâs some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical, and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects - 325 of them - are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consist of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nuclei. FSRQs represent a type of âblazarâ - a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy at this 20-200 MeV spectral window.

Fraser and Pamela discuss the differnet "colors" of gamma rays.

Closer to home, the catalogue includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars - the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time itâs ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, are the 73 sources that donât have a clear counterpart at other energies. 60 of those appear to be brand new gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the dataset awaiting follow-up observations. One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China, and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data of this satellite, which was originally launched in 2008. However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASAâs Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2-5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades worth of Fermi might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.

#6410. A Five-Day Experiment Reveals a Surprising Secret of Deadly Brain Cancer

Researchers tracking glioblastoma cells in living mouse brain tissue discovered how quickly they can change their paths, revealing a hidden challenge in stopping this aggressive brain cancer.

Glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, largely because its cells can spread deep into surrounding healthy tissue. Even after surgeons remove the main tumor, scattered cancer cells may remain in the brain and eventually contribute to the disease returning.

Understanding how these cells spread has been difficult because researchers have largely relied on images that capture only individual moments. Scientists at Uppsala University have now developed a method that lets them watch thousands of glioblastoma cells move through living brain tissue, revealing how they change their behavior over time. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help researchers better understand why this cancer is so difficult to contain.

“Until now, we have mostly seen snapshots of how glioblastoma spreads. This method combines microscopy with artificial intelligence and allows us to watch the process unfold in living brain tissue. We could also compare tumors from different patients and investigate how they respond to treatment,” says Hitesh Mangukiya, researcher at the Department of Immunology, Genetics and Pathology at Uppsala University and one of the study’s lead authors.

The new method, called GlioTrace, combines automated microscopy with machine learning to follow individual cancer cells as they travel through brain tissue. To test it, the researchers collected glioblastoma cells from six patients and grew them as tumors in mouse brains. They then cut the brains into thin slices, kept the tissue alive in the laboratory, and photographed it at intervals of no more than two hours for up to five days.

A computer system identified and tracked individual tumor cells across the images, while statistical models helped researchers calculate when cells switched between different states. Unlike techniques that examine only small regions of the brain, GlioTrace can monitor cells across entire brain slices using standard microscopes.

The observations revealed that glioblastoma cells do not all spread in the same way. Some tumors showed a preference for traveling along blood vessels, while others spread more diffusely through the surrounding brain tissue. These differences were apparent between tumors derived from different patients.

Individual cells were also remarkably adaptable. A cancer cell moving along a blood vessel could later leave that route and travel independently through the tissue. Some cells changed their shape and movement patterns over just a few days, suggesting that their behavior is far less fixed than individual images might imply.

“What surprised us most was how flexible the tumor cells are. The same cell can change how it moves over just a few days. To develop treatments that stop tumor cells from spreading, we need to understand this ability to switch between different behaviors,” says Madeleine Skeppås, PhD student at Uppsala University and co-lead author of the study.

The team also used GlioTrace to examine how cancer treatments influence cell movement. Two drug substances reduced the movement and spread of tumor cells in the brain slices, although their effectiveness varied between patient-derived tumors. Even within the same research setting, cells with different movement patterns did not respond equally to the drugs.

Another experiment raised questions about what happens to invasive cells during treatment. In some tumor models, combining radiation with chemotherapy increased the proportion of cells with a particular shape. These cells were among the fastest moving and occupied a central position in the network of transitions between different cell states, indicating that they were closely connected to changes in cell behavior.

The findings suggest that certain highly invasive cells might persist during treatment. However, the researchers have not established whether these cells are more resistant to therapy or whether they contribute to tumor recurrence. Further studies will be needed to determine what this response means for treating glioblastoma.

“Using this method allows us to monitor, for the first time, how thousands of individual tumor cells move through living brain tissue and to see how they adapt their behavior in real time. It opens up new possibilities to understand and, in the long term, halt the invasion process,” says Sven Nelander, Professor of Integrative Cancer Research at Uppsala University.

An important part of GlioTrace is the computational analysis system developed by Skeppås together with colleagues at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. The software processes microscopy images, recognizes the different shapes of cancer cells, and estimates how their characteristics change over time. It has also been made freely available, allowing other researchers to investigate how tumor cells interact with their surroundings and respond to potential treatments.

Although GlioTrace offers a more detailed view of cancer cell invasion, it remains a laboratory research method rather than a tool for making clinical decisions.

“We hope that the method will help us understand how tumor cells interact with their surroundings and identify treatments that can prevent cancer from spreading through the brain. However, for now, GlioTrace is a research method, and further studies are needed before it could be used to guide treatment decisions in patients,” says Hitesh Mangukiya.

Reference: “Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion” by Hitesh Bhagavanbhai Mangukiya, Madeleine Skeppås, André Lasses Armatowski, Irem Uppman, Linnea Hallin, Filippa Kruse, Clara Nordquist, Soumi Kundu, Maria Berglund, Adam A. A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

#6407. Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity. Unlike stars like our Sun, which are relatively radio-quiet, red dwarfs (M dwarfs) can produce strong radio emissions. A team of astronomers used that to their advantage to take precision measurements of a binary pair of M dwarfs about 59 million light years from Earth. They determined the stars' orbits and masses with uncommon accuracy.

One fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger. Stars inherit angular momentum from their formation in gas clouds, and since M dwarfs are so small, that momentum is concentrated, making them spin rapidly. They eventually slow down, but this initial rapid rotation makes them very active.

The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.

One subset of young M dwarfs is even more extreme. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. They're M dwarfs that display complex, periodical optical light curves with sharp drops rather than smooth drops found in most stellar light curves. Their drops aren't simple; there can be multiple dips and peaks during a single rotation. Astrophysicists call their light curves multi-harmonic, and the patterns repeat across multiple rotations.

This image shows CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. Notice the sharp drops in the curves rather than typical smooth drops found in other stellar light curves. Image Credit: Bouma et al. 2023. AnJ

The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star. Though CPV stars have complex light curves generated by their youthful, rapid rotation, their youthfulness also means they're radio loud. In fact, since both of these stars are young M dwarfs, they're both radio loud. That helped the researchers measure them with such accuracy.

The measurments of DG CVn are in new research in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Accurate dynamical mass and orbit determination of the M dwarf binary DG CVn using astrometric very long baseline interferometry." The lead author is Paul VLBI , a network system engineer at the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry ERIC (JIVE), and a Leiden Observatory PhD student. It's noteworthy that this is the first mass measurement of a system with a CPV star.

"We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star." - Boven et al. 2026.

The astronomers' results are based on observations that spanned 18 years. Observations with the National Science Foundationâs Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) between 2023 and 2025 were especially important in their precise results. The VLBA is a system of 10 radiotelescopes across the USA, each one measuring 25 meters. The 10 dishes work as an interferometer, and the VLBA has the longest baseline in the world, up to 8,611 km long.

"Astrometry through very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) allows the monitoring of radio-loud stars and the detection of any reflex motion due to stellar or substellar companions," the authors write. Reflex motion is the characteristic gravitational wobble induced in a star when a companion tugs on it.

That wobble is often used to detect unseeable exoplanets orbiting stars. Even a small planet can make its star wobble, and that's at the heart of the radial velocity method of detecting exoplanet. The DG CVn system was actually found when astronomers were searching for exoplanets with the radial velocity method. But the system exhibited a more powerful and complex wobble than an exoplanet would.

âWe were really lucky to hear about this object when we had developed tools with which we could explain these motions,â said Boven. âBut the real surprise came when we also detected the second radio-loud dwarf in the observations we did to confirm our model. It really allowed us to measure the system very precisely.â

Measuring reflex motion accurately with the VLBI let the astronomers track the stars' paths, including the tiny wobbles, which in turn let them understand the mass of the stars with extreme precision.

This figure from the research shows the VLBI detections of both members of DG CVn, and their modeled motion across the sky. The dates mark the predicted positions of DG CVn B over time. The inset image shows recent observations when both sources were detected. Image Credit: Boven et al. 2026. A&A.

"In our recent observations, we reliably detected both binary components," the authors write. "A unique and accurate determination of the 1647.647 Â± 0.027 day orbit, with a parallax distance of 18.1851 Â± 0.0033 pc (about 59 light years), is presented. The dynamical masses were estimated with a precision of 0.16% from the sampled posteriors."

The pair of stars orbit each other every 4.511 years on an elongated elliptical orbit. When they're closest to one another, they're only separated by 0.59 astronomical units. DG CVn A is the more massive of the pair with 0.39 solar masses, while DG CVn B has 0.36 solar masses. The pair is close enough to measure their distance with parallax, which gives accurate measurements.

The red dwarfs and their radio emissions are central to this work. The stars are simply too close together from this distance to be separated in optical observations. But the VLBA can pinpoint their locations with extreme accuracy. All of this work let the researchers characterize the system in clear detail, following the motions of both stars through the sky separately.

âDG CVn is a beautiful example of what precise radio astrometry can reveal,â said Jay Blanchard, NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory astronomer and study co-author. âBy following these two stars over many years, we can see their orbital motion directly and use that motion to determine properties that would otherwise be extremely difficult to measure.â

These accurate measurements also tell astronomers about their planetary systems. Planets form in protoplanetary disks around stars, and since these stars are so close together, that limits the size of their disks. Smaller disks mean smaller planets, so that limits the size of any exoplanets in the system. It's also extremely unlikely that any long-period planets are orbiting either star.

According to the researchers' estimates, an exoplanet in orbit around one of the stars could only be in a stable orbit if its orbital period was less than approximately 23 days. For a circumbinary planet orbiting both stars, the orbital period would have to be at least about 36 years. These approximations are also important, because they can refine the understanding of how exoplanets can form and survive in binary star systems.

Gaia's Data Release 4 is due in a couple of weeks, and it will include binary star parameters for the mission's complete survey. But that data alone won't be able to differentiate between binaries where both are low mass stars, and binaries where one might be a massive planet. But the VLBI will be able to address that. "Astrometric follow-up of selected detections with VLBI can help to differentiate between binary star systems and reflex motion due to large exoplanets (or even both)," the authors write.

"We have presented a complete binary orbital solution with high accuracy based on VLBI astrometry of a binary that is difficult to resolve for optical telescopes on the ground or in orbit," the authors write. "The absolute astrometry provided by VLBI allowed the individual dynamical masses to be determined with high accuracy. These results show that VLBI is well suited for studying the orbits of radio-loud stars."

The results also show how powerful the combination of archival observations and new observations can be. "The value of combining archival and recent VLBI astrometric observations has been demonstrated. It resulted in a highly accurate determination of the system composition, orbit, position, and distance," the authors write. "We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star."

The VLBI network of radio dishes is about to have a growth spurt when the Square Kilometre Array and the Next Generation Very Large Array come online. That will improve the system's reach and precision.

"In the future, we hope to make measurements precise enough to detect planets in orbit around such radio-loud dwarfs,â said Huib van Langevelde, chief scientist a the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry and Leiden Observatory professor. âWe think that when the ngVLA and the SKA become part of the VLBI network, we can do even more precise measurements, for many more, more distant stars.â

#6406. A Common Gut Antibody May Be the Key to Preventing Colon Cancer Before It Starts

People who lack a common gut antibody face higher colorectal cancer risk, and experiments in mice are beginning to explain how that missing protection may matter.

Long before colon cancer develops, cells lining the intestine can begin dividing too quickly. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that a common gut antibody helps keep this growth under control in mice, raising the possibility of preventing tumors before they form.

In a study published in Nature, mice lacking immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal antibody levels. Giving the deficient mice IgA by mouth eliminated their increased cancer risk.

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 Americans, face a higher risk of colorectal cancer.

“One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer,” says senior author Daniel Mucida, head of Rockefeller’s Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. “Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?”

IgA is one of the immune system’s first lines of defense. Unlike antibodies that target specific pathogens, it can bind to many kinds of gut bacteria and even some healthy human cells. Scientists have long known that these antibodies are abundant in the digestive system, although their full purpose has remained unclear.

Gregory Donaldson, a former Rockefeller postdoctoral fellow who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, investigated whether IgA’s interactions with gut bacteria could explain its connection to cancer. He compared mice lacking IgA with normal mice raised alongside them, ensuring both groups encountered the same food and germs.

The increased cancer risk appeared across several different models of colon cancer. More importantly, the researchers found changes in genes controlling cell division before any tumors developed, suggesting that IgA influences cancer risk at an early stage.

The team traced this effect to DMBT1, a receptor on the surface of intestinal cells. Gabriella Lima dos Reis, a graduate student in Gabriel Victora’s laboratory, helped identify its role.

In the presence of gut bacteria, DMBT1 encourages intestinal cells to multiply. IgA acts like a brake by binding to the receptor and limiting that growth. Without IgA, the signal can become overactive, allowing cells to divide excessively and form tumors. The researchers found that removing gut bacteria or DMBT1 signaling also prevented this uncontrolled growth.

“If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function—responding to bacteria by producing new cells—can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer,” Mucida says. “We think this homeostatic effect is IgA’s main function. This was a big surprise.”

The discovery could eventually lead to new ways of reducing colon cancer risk, particularly for people who have had polyps removed. Polyps increase the likelihood of developing colon cancer, and Mucida believes targeting this pathway could offer a way to lower that risk.

Donaldson also sees potential in beneficial gut bacteria. Although much research has focused on microbes that encourage tumor growth, some bacteria may help protect intestinal cells. One possibility is developing probiotics that stimulate protective IgA responses.

Both approaches remain speculative, and the findings have not established a cancer-prevention treatment for humans. However, the study suggests that understanding how gut bacteria, antibodies, and intestinal cells interact could reveal new opportunities to prevent cancer before it starts.

Reference: “Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA” by Gregory P. Donaldson, Gabriella Lima dos Reis, Marwa Saad, Christopher Wichmann, Izabela Mamede, Guo Chen, Caroline E. Harrer, Nicole L. DelGaudio, Dayu Zhang, Begüm Aydin, Tiago B. R. Castro, Sergei I. Grivennikov, Bernardo S. Reis, Elise G. Liu, Stephanie C. Eisenbarth, Kivanç Birsoy, Sohail F. Tavazoie, Beth M. Stadtmueller, Gabriel D. Victora and Daniel Mucida, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2

#6404. Scientists Discover Alarming Signs of Extinction Risk Deep Beneath the Ocean

A changing ocean presents threats that population counts alone may not reveal, and genetic evidence from the Gulf suggests some deep-sea species are already vulnerable.

The deep ocean may no longer be the safe haven scientists once believed it was. Hundreds of meters beneath the Gulf’s surface, fish and shrimp are showing genetic warning signs linked to extinction risk, raising concerns that the global biodiversity crisis could threaten even some of the ocean’s most remote inhabitants.

A new study led by researchers at Florida International University (FIU) found evidence that five deep-sea species may be less resilient to environmental change than previously assumed. Led by FIU marine scientist Pedro A. Peres of the Bracken-Grissom Lab, the research examined three species of lanternfish and two species of deep-sea shrimp collected between 2011 and 2023.

The team analyzed genetic information from 486 specimens to investigate how these populations had changed and whether they could withstand future environmental pressures. According to Peres, the investigation is among only a handful of studies to track changes in the DNA of deep-sea animals over time.

All five species showed genetic warning signs associated with increased extinction risk. One lanternfish species, Diaphus dumerilii, had lost approximately 8% of its genetic diversity over just 12 years. That decline was comparable to, or greater than, losses recorded in some threatened and endangered animals over considerably longer periods.

The researchers also discovered that all five species had relatively small effective population sizes. This measure does not necessarily reflect how many animals are alive. Instead, it describes how many individuals effectively contribute their genes to future generations. A species can therefore have a large population while relying on a much smaller group to maintain its genetic diversity.

“This challenges the idea that deep-sea species are naturally more resilient because they occupy such vast environments,” Peres said. “It shows how much we can miss when we look only at population abundance without considering their genetic diversity and long-term viability.”

Genetic diversity helps explain why these findings matter. When individuals within a species carry different genetic traits, their population has more opportunities to adapt as conditions change. Losing that variation can make it harder to survive disease, environmental disturbances, and other threats.

Heather Bracken-Grissom, assistant director of the Institute of Environment’s Coastlines and Oceans Division, has spearheaded research into the genetic diversity and resilience of deep-sea species. As a co-author of the new study, she emphasized the consequences of losing that diversity.

“Genetic diversity provides the variation populations need to adapt to changing conditions, resist disease and recover from environmental disturbances,” she said. “When that diversity disappears, a species can also lose the ability to withstand future threats.”

The genetic findings are especially concerning when considered alongside predictions about the Gulf’s future. Using climate models, the researchers estimated how suitable deep-sea habitats could become for these species by 2050 and 2100. Their projections indicated that four of the five species could experience substantial reductions in suitable habitat, potentially losing as much as 70%.

Such losses could place additional pressure on populations already showing signs of limited genetic resilience. The possibility challenges a longstanding assumption that deep-sea animals are naturally protected by their extensive habitats and broad geographic distributions.

The findings also raise questions about the lasting consequences of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Earlier research documented substantial declines in deep-sea animal populations following the disaster, although the precise relationship between that event and the genetic patterns identified in the new study remains uncertain.

The researchers did not establish that the oil spill caused the genetic changes they observed. Their results instead suggest that some populations may have been vulnerable even before the disaster, potentially making environmental disturbances more consequential.

“Our results suggest some deep-sea populations may have already been genetically vulnerable before the Deepwater Horizon oil spill,” Peres said. “This has important implications for understanding the consequences of environmental disturbances. Events such as oil spills may affect populations that already have limited genetic resilience.”

The study, which also included FIU researcher Keith Sellers and Tracey T. Sutton of Nova Southeastern University, points to a gap in how scientists assess the health of marine ecosystems. Traditional surveys can reveal changes in population numbers, yet they may overlook genetic vulnerabilities that affect whether those populations can survive over the long term.

By examining DNA across multiple years, researchers can identify threats that might remain hidden in ordinary population counts. Peres believes this approach should become a greater priority as scientists work to understand the pressures facing deep-sea life.

“This study serves as a wake-up call for the scientific community,” Peres said, “highlighting the urgent need to integrate genetic monitoring into biodiversity assessments and emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring to better understand and detect changes in marine populations over time.”

Reference: “Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling” by Pedro A. Peres, Keith Sellers, Tracey T. Sutton and Heather Bracken-Grissom, 12 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79098-0

This research was funded in part by a grant from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s RESTORE Science Program (ROR – https://ror.org/0042xzm63) under awards NA19NOS4510193-T1-01 and NA24NOSX451C0002-T1-01 to Nova Southeastern University, in part by a grant from The Gulf of Mexico Research Initiative (GoMRI), and in part by the NOAA Office of Response and Restoration.

#6403. Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

Scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

Unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is currently a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

SwRI - SwRI team studies interior composition, origins of ice giants

O. Mousis et al - Primordial and Radiogenic Argon 40 in Uranus and Neptune

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

Dhungana, S., & Flament, N. (2026). The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature, 659(8139), 106–112. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6401. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6400. A Simple Cable Reveals Hidden Cracks That Could Weaken Glaciers From Within

A single fiber-optic cable can turn a glacier’s faint vibrations into a map of its inner structure, helping scientists assess how likely it is to break apart.

Cracks hidden inside glaciers can play a critical role in their collapse. Meltwater can drive these fractures deeper into the ice, weakening glaciers that may appear intact from above. Satellites and drones can map surface features, but they cannot reveal the full extent of the damage within.

The consequences of glacier failure have become painfully clear in the Alps. In July 2022, a collapse on Italy’s Marmolada Glacier killed 11 mountaineers. In May 2025, Switzerland’s Birch Glacier collapsed above Blatten, drawing international attention.

Now, researchers at ETH Zurich have demonstrated a potentially simpler and less expensive way to examine hidden fractures in much greater detail. Their study, led by Assistant Professor Thomas Hudson of the Environmental and Exploration Geophysics Group, appears in Science Advances.

Opening crevasses produce tiny earthquakes, sending vibrations through the surrounding ice. Scientists can record these signals with seismometers and trace them back to their sources. Getting a detailed picture, however, requires many instruments, which are costly and difficult to install across a glacier crisscrossed by dangerous cracks.

For their experiment, Hudson and his colleagues laid a single fiber-optic cable across the Gorner Glacier in Switzerland’s canton of Valais. They used it to investigate the glacier’s interior down to 25 meters (82 feet). “A single fiber-optic cable replaces hundreds of seismometers,” emphasizes Hudson.

The cable connects to an instrument called an interrogator, which sends light through the fiber and measures the light scattered back. Seismic waves from a cracking glacier slightly stretch or compress sections of the cable, changing the returning light signal. These changes allow researchers to locate the vibrations and determine how deep their sources lie.

Computational methods turn the recordings into a picture of the glacier’s internal structure and composition, somewhat like a medical ultrasound scan. The measurements generate enormous amounts of data, requiring substantial computing power and an algorithm to help interpret them.

The survey revealed that water-filled or air-filled crevasses occupied more than eight percent of the ice volume at the study site. Approximately 92 percent remained intact. “That’s far more than we expected,” says Hudson.

The result shows why a glacier’s appearance can offer an incomplete picture of its stability. “Laypeople often assume that large, visible surface crevasses indicate whether a glacier is stable or not. However, scientists pay more attention to internal cracks and crevasses inside the ice,” Hudson explains.

Mapping that damage could help researchers assess the risk of calving, when pieces of ice break away from a glacier. The technique could eventually support monitoring of unstable glaciers and provide earlier warnings of major breakoffs at their fronts.

“We are very pleased with the test runs on the Gorner Glacier. The method has proven its worth,” Hudson says.

Crevasses also influence how a glacier moves. Water entering these openings can reach the bed beneath the ice, where it can act as a lubricant and potentially accelerate the glacier’s slide. A fracture network can therefore affect both the strength of the ice and its overall behavior.

The effects extend far beyond mountain valleys to Greenland and Antarctica, where ice loss from enormous ice sheets contributes to rising seas. Understanding how fractures develop and carry water through those ice sheets could help scientists better anticipate their response to changing conditions.

The ETH team plans to test the technique on other glaciers in the Swiss Alps and on polar ice sheets. By combining measurements from within the ice with satellite observations of the surface, the researchers hope to track how crevasses develop over time and space and how shallow cracks connect with deeper fractures.

“Our method could therefore help to predict changes in the ice sheets and sea levels,” Hudson explains.

Reference: “Quantifying subsurface fracture damage in glaciers using fiber-optic seismology” by Thomas S. Hudson, Fabian Walter, Sebastian Noe, Andrea Zunino, John-Michael Kendall, Pascal Edme and Andreas Fichtner, 23 July 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef1107

#6399. For the First Time, Scientists Capture Molecular-Scale Images of the Poles of Bacteria

Scientists have captured the first molecular-resolution images of the ends of rod-shaped bacteria, revealing previously unseen structural features.

Scientists have captured the ends of living, rod-shaped bacteria at molecular resolution for the first time, exposing surface structures that were previously impossible to examine in such detail. The images reveal differences in bacterial architecture that could help researchers understand why some species respond to antibiotics differently from others.

The breakthrough, led by researchers at UCL (University College London) and published in Nature Communications, relied on an unexpected discovery: bacteria attached to a specially treated glass surface could remain standing upright, allowing scientists to examine their exposed tips, known as poles.

To keep bacterial cells from moving during imaging, the researchers coated glass with a chemical that binds to proteins on their surfaces. The technique held the bacteria securely without preventing them from growing or reproducing, overcoming a major obstacle to studying living cells at extremely high resolution.

After 20 minutes, the bacteria were generally immobilized horizontally. When left for longer (about 50 minutes), many unexpectedly stood upright, exposing the ends of their cells for direct examination.

The team used atomic force microscopy to image these surfaces. Unlike conventional light microscopes, this technology uses a probe just a few nanometers wide that gently taps across the cell, detecting its contours much like a finger reading Braille. The resulting measurements reveal structural details far smaller than those visible with ordinary light microscopy.

The images showed that bacterial poles change with cellular activity. Rapidly dividing bacteria (i.e., ones that were dividing rapidly) had fold-like defects at their ends, while less active cells generally displayed smoother, more rounded poles. These irregularities suggest that the bacterial surface may not have fully remodeled after cell division.

The researchers also examined E. coli (Escherichia coli) alongside Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii, species associated with difficult-to-treat infections. Unlike E. coli, the other two bacteria lacked the network of tiny openings (pores) observed on its surface. These structural differences may influence how the species interact with antibiotics, although their precise effects on drug susceptibility remain to be established.

Lead author Dr. Anna Scheeder, based at the London Centre for Nanotechnology at UCL, said: “Our immobilization method opens up exciting new possibilities. We can now study the armor of bacteria across different species more reliably and clearly observe nanoscale differences that were previously difficult to assess.”

Bacterial poles are closely connected to cell division, when new ends form as a bacterium splits into two daughter cells. Some antibiotics preferentially act on these regions, making their molecular structure a potential source of information for developing new treatments.

Senior author Professor Bart Hoogenboom (London Centre for Nanotechnology at UCL and UCL Physics and Astronomy) said: “Imaging the poles of bacteria is like opening a view of the back of the moon. We are looking at something that no one else has seen before. The poles are where cells divide and so contain critical information about this process. They may also be a particular target for antibiotics, with some bacteria-killing treatments preferring to attack this part of the cell.

“Our method of immobilizing the cells without affecting their ability to grow and reproduce also means we can image a much larger range of live bacteria than was previously possible. This is important as it may help us understand differences between species and why antibiotics work for some of them but not others.

“Our work is fundamental science that ultimately aims to find new leads to target drug-resistant bacteria.”

Reference: “Nanometer-resolution imaging of living bacteria across species and cellular orientations” by Anna Scheeder, Joanna Szczepaniak, Yulianna Koziy, Naomi Mara Claro De Oliveira, William Trewby, Renata Kaminska, Jeremy Brown, Colin Kleanthous and Bart W. Hoogenboom, 9 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78975-y

The work was funded by the Wellcome Trust, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), the Rosetrees Trust, and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC).

#6398. The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

The Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

We live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

But another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

This image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Big Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

The stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Big Bang theory of cosmology.

Other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. Currently, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an important discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Big Bang theory.

The South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466

But there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Big Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

This is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its big new deep and detailed maps,â says Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

This time-lapse shows the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger

The observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

It'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â says Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a new benchmark for observations.

The SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â says Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

The SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

This cut-away schematic shows the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

The SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs says. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â

This is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin says. âThis enables us to observe entirely new classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

But detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin says.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs says. Those images are uncovering new observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin says. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â

The SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.
