#6370. Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

"We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," said Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking said.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space. Science, eaea5324. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aea5324

#6363. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call)

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

#6362. I’m a Neurosurgeon. My Near-Death Experience Showed Me ‘Universal Consciousness’ for the First Time.

By comparison, it makes our material world feel “murky.”

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When I earned my medical degree at Duke University, I was taught that consciousness is created out of chemical reactions occurring within the brain, a foundational assumption of scientific materialism, or physicalism—the notion that only the physical exists. After eleven years of rigorous training, I practiced as a neurosurgeon for more than two decades, including 15 years teaching and operating at Harvard Medical School.

I performed surgical procedures that took patients from extreme discomfort to full relief by releasing a nerve blockage or removing a tumor. I could stimulate the brain in conscious patients and affect their mental experience, which initially seemed to support my physicalist worldview. At the same time, patients deeply comatose from brain maladies would sometimes become fully alert right before dying. I couldn’t explain these phenomena, and so I dismissed them. That is, until November 2008, when a severe case of bacterial meningitis caused me to spend seven days in deep coma—and later reshaped my view of the universe.

Over three hours, I went from back pain and headache to epileptic fits and coma, as E. coli bacteria devoured my neocortex, or the outer surface of the brain, the part that is most responsible for human mentation. Healthcare professionals use the Glasgow Coma Scale to measure decreases in consciousness, with scores less than 9 indicating deep coma. A corpse would score a 3, the lowest grade on the scale, and my scores were 6 to 7 during most of that week—the doctor was out! Lumbar puncture revealed my cerebrospinal fluid to be filled with pus under pressure, and the glucose level in that fluid was only 1 mg/dl (normally 80-90, with severe bacterial meningitis occasionally as low as 20). CT and MRI scans revealed my entire neocortex was involved, meaning there was no physical functioning brain left to produce a dream or hallucination.

By the tenets of modern neuroscience, my awareness should have been zero. Without a functioning neocortex, my brain was incapable of producing a simple thought or image—and yet, I lived through a vivid, richly-detailed, hyper-real event, by comparison making this material world appear murky and dreamlike. I was unbound by space and time, immersed in universal consciousness, and wrapped in unconditional love. I had visions revealing structure to the non-physical realm that fully relates to and intertwines with our lives here on earth.

Back in the hospital, my prospects for survival were down to 2 percent when, on day seven, I startled everyone as I began to awaken. My doctors were even more surprised when I fully recovered over about two months. As my medical knowledge returned, I reviewed my records and scans, and discussed them with my doctors, trying to make sense of it all. I searched for a physicalist explanation, yet the case was unyielding—no conventional explanation could suffice. I was forced to acknowledge that an expansive model of reality was required to explain my experience.

In 2018, when my case records were peer-reviewed before publication in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the editors asked the authors to explain my unprecedented recovery. They replied that my miraculous recovery occurred because of my spiritual journey, knowing of similar extraordinary recoveries in the near-death literature. Due to techniques of cardiac resuscitation developed in the 1960s, millions of others have escaped the shackles of the physical brain and body, and reported similar near-death experiences (NDEs) of connection with a non-physical realm. Those descriptions have been categorized and evaluated using Greyson’s NDE Scale (developed by UVA psychiatrist Bruce Greyson), which quantifies the cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental aspects of the experiences.

The vast evidence from these unusual experiences has convinced many former physicalists that their model is outdated. A more sufficient explanation is that the brain serves as a transceiver or antenna for tuning in to a larger, collective consciousness. Renowned Harvard psychologist William James, French philosopher Henri Bergson, and English writer Aldous Huxley, all postulated this “reducing valve” role for the brain in the early 20th century, noting that a shift in the primary physicalist assumption was required to explain these phenomena.

With a growing abundance of data, it is clearer that consciousness is fundamental and influences physical matter from the top down, rather than the bottom-up model of physicalism, where consciousness arises from the brain. Spontaneous remissions and the placebo effect confirm the power of the mind over matter and validate the observer effect seen in quantum mechanics experiments.

The “hard problem of consciousness” remains unsolved because its underlying premise is false.

I believe merging first-person subjective inquiry with rigorous empirical science will take us farther in knowing the true nature of our consensus reality.

To that point, humanity will thrive when science finally acknowledges that we are interconnected through love and part of one larger consciousness, with free will to become the best version of ourselves, both as individuals and collectively. The golden rule is woven directly into the fabric of the universe, providing a moral compass that shows that, ultimately, what matters most is how we treat each other.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6358. Humans Have Used the Same Comb Design Since the Stone Age. This One Might Finally Beat Baldness.

Named after Disney’s Tangled, this comb zaps hair-growth molecules straight into shrinking follicles.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The oldest-known comb, fashioned from animal bone, dates back nearly 8,000 years to mesolithic Syria. But in those intervening 10,000 years, the comb hasn’t seen much innovation. Sure, plastics have long since replaced bone as the material of choice for this particular piece of grooming gear (though animal bone combs are still a thing). But the comb’s overall shape and function—individual tines and all—has remained remarkably unchanged.

“The basic design evolved from the fingers of the human hand,” the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford writes on its website. “From Bronze-Age man to Cleopatra, to Napoleon's wife, Josephine, all would recognize these items as such.”

But just because something’s remained largely unchanged for millennia doesn’t mean there isn’t room for innovation. Take, for instance, the “Detangle,” an experimental comb developed by Beihang University in China as a tool for tackling androgenetic alopecia (AGA), or just simply baldness. At first glance, the comb looks much like any other hand-inspired comb—there’s a long handle and the recognizable tines. However, that’s where the similarities end, because this comb has teeth packed with embedded electrodes as well as small compartments for delivering molecules designed to stimulate hair growth. Researchers published a study detailing the efficacy of this experimental comb in the journal Nature Communications.

“Androgenetic alopecia affects over 1.5 billion individuals, causing progressive hair loss with psychological and quality-of-life burdens,” the authors write. “This system features electronic teeth embedded with height-differentiated electrodes and integrated drug-loading modules, which generate an enhanced electric field penetrating up to ~9 times deeper into hair follicle regions than conventional external application.”

This “Detangle” device, whose name the authors admit was inspired by the Disney animated film Tangled, isn’t a new hair-loss treatment so much as a revolutionary way to deliver one. One of its most high-tech features is a control circuit that creates pulsed electric fields across two types of electronic teeth. These teeth have different heights that generate a stronger electric field than if the teeth were aligned. That generates a positive environment for the transmembrane delivery of a therapeutic molecule into the impacted follicular cells, increasing uptake by more than three times, the authors report.

The authors tested the comb on mouse models and found hair growth recovered near 100 percent within a month, a steep increase from the approximate 70 percent recovery rate of typical minoxidil treatments—one of the go-to FDA-approved treatments for hair loss. To achieve this impressive recovery rate, the authors relied on the SRD5A2 siRNA molecule and a VEGFA plasmid. The first molecule inhibits dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone that causes hair follicles to shrink, while the latter boosts blood vessel growth around the impacted follicles.

“By co‑delivering VEGFA plasmid and SRD5A2 siRNA, the Detangle system promotes hair follicle regeneration via a dual mechanism that synergizes electrostimulation with molecular regulation,” the authors write. “Given the multifaceted signaling abnormalities in AGA, the Detangle system presents a versatile platform for co‑delivering therapeutic agents beyond metabolic modulation.”

After 10,000 years, the comb finally gets a serious glow up.

#6356. Ancient Egyptians Revered Cats as Sacred. Then 131 Skulls Revealed What Really Happened to Them.

Fractured skulls, healed wounds, and signs of strangling suggest sacred cats lived—and died—brutally.

Not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans. Across Egypt, the cemeteries of Bubastis in the eastern Nile Delta, the Bubasteion in northern Saqqara, and Speos Artemidos near Beni Hassan, along with others in Giza and the Dakhla Oasis, were meant for animals, especially cats. Cats were seen as the earthly embodiment of the feline goddess Bastet. Yet although they were often mummified as votive offerings, their treatment did not always match their status.

Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties. Some animal mummies were used as ship ballast for the journey home after an expedition, while others were powdered for questionable medicine, burned for fuel, or ground into fertilizer. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, however, some animal mummies were unwrapped (without a party) so that their skeletal remains could inform studies of Egyptian fauna. Many of these skulls remain in museum collections in Egypt and abroad. Zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences and his research team studied one such collection: 131 exceptionally well-preserved skulls of small cats from Beni Hassan, now housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Their goal was to find out how the cats lived before they died.

“Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science. In addition to carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis to determine diet, “characteristics such as dental abnormalities, infectious or metabolic disorders and trauma were recorded.”

Most of the skulls turned out to be from domestic cats (Felis catus), with several jungle cats (Felis chaus) among them. Many of the animals apparently suffered from conditions such as gum disease and infections, and some skulls had puncture marks and fractures that could indicate fights between cats. How the cats met their end, however, was more disturbing. Evidence suggests that cats were deliberately killed so they could be turned into offerings to Bastet. Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma. Sharp-force trauma is thought to have possibly killed the humans who were sacrificed to join First Dynasty pharaohs in the afterlife. Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.

When Van Neer and his team took a closer look at one skull, they found marks consistent with blows from a sharp metal weapon. Wounds on some of the other skulls were thought to have been made by strikes from a heavy wooden implement. The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today. Isotope analysis showed that the jungle cats’ diet clearly differed from that of the domestic cats, further suggesting that this species was unlikely to have been bred in captivity.

Even among the wild-caught jungle cats, six of the seven skulls came from animals with conditions similar to those of their domestic relatives. This was probably a sign that all of the cats, the overwhelming majority of which were adults, were kept in conditions that caused illness and injury before death. Radiocarbon dating revealed when they died.

Cats are generally thought to have first been domesticated in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East roughly 10,000 years ago, although some recent genetic studies suggest it happened later, in Egypt or elsewhere in North Africa. In Egypt, the earliest clear evidence of domestic cats dates to the Middle Kingdom (c. 2000–1700 B.C.E.). However, demand for mummified cat offerings was greatest much later, in the Late and Ptolemaic Periods. Older feline mummies do exist, and one of the nine dated skulls goes back to the Third Intermediate Period. The other eight, however, date to between 380 and 40 B.C.E., from the end of the Late Period into the Ptolemaic era.

As for how the cats were killed, blunt- or sharp-force trauma appears to have been the main cause of death. Some cats were strangled, but a blow to the head was apparently the more common method. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers said. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”

She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6355. Trump names Stephen Miller his chief of staff ahead of Dem takeover

Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”

Wiles, who Trump recently announced had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

Miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once said the party is “unworthy of power.”

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller said during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6352. Why Do Helmets Still Fail to Stop Concussions? Scientists May Have Been Fighting the Wrong Force All Along.

A WWII physicist said twisting hits were the real danger. Sensors in 203 athletes’ mouths say otherwise.

An estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S. each year. They’re so common that you might assume they’re not as serious as other injuries—but in fact, these mild traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) can often be more dangerous. While tendons, muscle, and bone heal good as new, repeated and sustained concussions—a typical occurrence in many athletic endeavors—can lead to dementia and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), an aggressive degenerative brain disease.

Although helmets have grown safer over the years in certain sports, concussions are still commonplace. That’s especially true in football, even after the high-profile introduction of the Guardian Cap for NFL preseason practices in 2022 and then in regular-season games in 2024. This suggests that there’s something about concussions, specifically the relationship of linear and rotational acceleration and the brain, that scientists still don’t understand.

During World War II, Scottish physicist A.H.S. Holbourn argued that rotational acceleration (think of an uppercut to the jaw) was more dangerous than linear acceleration (a straight-on, direct hit whose force goes through the center of the head). His theory was that rotation was worse because it stretches and strains brain tissue by moving different parts at different speeds. Scientists have focused on protecting against rotation ever since.

However, a new Stanford Medicine-led study suggests that linear acceleration, not rotation, may be the better predictor of concussion. The research comes from the lab of bioengineer David Camarillo, who’s spent more than a decade studying concussions and helmet safety. By analyzing unprecedentedly accurate impact data from motion-sensing mouthguards worn by 203 athletes across seven different sports, Camarillo and his team discovered that Holbourn’s initial assumptions weren’t correct. The results of their study were published in the journal Annals of Biomedical Engineering.

“Holbourn’s reasoning was based just on mechanics; it wasn’t biology,” David Camarillo, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “The question we started out with many years ago was, ‘What are the forces required to cause concussion?’ If we understand the nature of those forces and the limits of the human brain, then it might be possible to prevent concussions.”

Previous studies relied on helmet-mounted sensors, but the authors note that those sensors are often inaccurate because helmets tend to move around a lot. Across the mouthguard-enabled data set, the researchers analyzed 3,851 impacts, of which 47 were verified as concussions. In their mathematical models comparing the data, peak linear acceleration was the single most predictive factor in whether a hit eventually produced a concussion. Camarillo and his team haven’t pinned down a mechanism for this result, but they suspect one of two culprits: the brain striking the inside of the skull, or cavitation, in which sudden pressure changes form tiny bubbles that then collapse.

If these results hold up in future studies, they could have profound implications for helmet safety and design. The mouthguard data showed that a hit producing 100 g of linear acceleration (100 times the acceleration of gravity) carries a 50 percent risk of concussion. That’s far lower than the often-cited 192 g threshold from earlier helmet-sensor studies. At 150 g, a hit that older data would have considered below the danger line, concussion risk tops 99 percent.

“Why are there so many concussions even when people are wearing helmets?” Camarillo asked. “Part of the answer could be in this paper, which is that the linear accelerations that we previously thought were safe, we now see are much more dangerous.”

In a way, the new results offer a bit of hope that helmets do have room for improvement, and with a greater focus on addressing linear acceleration, concussions could significantly drop in the coming years and decades. One Stanford-developed technology is a helmet with liquid-filled pads that reduces peak linear acceleration and knocks nearly 20 percentage points off the chances of concussion on high-impact hits versus standard football helmets.

“If linear acceleration is its own distinct mechanism of concussion and it’s very common, then we’ve been missing a lot,” Camarillo said. “We haven’t tried as hard to optimize for this variable. It gives me some hope that there’s a new opportunity for preventing concussions.”

#6350. Archaeologists Found a Castaway Camp on an Island at the End of the World. Did a Legendary Sailor Build It?

The island behind a Jules Verne classic was hiding a shipwreck mystery.

While hunting penguins for oil (yes, people really do that) in 1873, famed Argentine sailor Luis Piedra Buena wrecked his schooner brig Espora off the southern tip of South America. He and his crew regrouped on a deserted beach, spent about two months building a new cutter, the Luisito, and sailed safely to Chile to tell their tale. Now, researchers believe they may have found pieces of a shipwreck and the remains of a “castaway camp” possibly tied to Piedra Buena on Isla de los Estados, an island “at the end of the world.”

In a new study published in the journal Antiquity, lead author Nicolás Ciarlo of Spain’s University of Cádiz and his colleagues describe how their research into the maritime history of the island, which lies across the Strait of Le Maire from the tip of Tierra del Fuego, led them to a castaway camp. They believe the camp may link the island’s Lacroix Inlet in Franklin Bay to the more than 150-year-old survival story.

Isla de los Estados is probably best known for a lighthouse that inspired Jules Verne’s novel The Lighthouse at the End of the World. The island forms the easternmost point of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego Province, and from the 17th century onward it lay along a key sailing route.

By 1870, the Argentine government had granted the island to Piedra Buena. Although he never established a settlement there, he sailed past it countless times while pursuing his interests throughout Patagonia. Then disaster struck. “During a campaign for exploiting penguins for oil, he and his crew lost the schooner brig Espora,” according to the study.

The crew survived, built a cutter, and sailed to Punta Arenas, Chile. There, Piedra Buena described the time they had spent at Lacroix Inlet, although experts have long doubted that he identified the location correctly.

To test his account, the research team visited Lacroix Inlet in January 2026 with help from the Argentine Navy. There, they found the “remains of a shipwreck and a temporary camp” on a wind-battered stretch of coast at the base of a cliff, exposed to strong southwesterly storms. The “possible castaway camp” sat near a stream.

“Although there is still no common agreement, Piedra Buena’s account and other documentary evidence suggest that this bay is likely the place where the Espora sank,” the authors wrote. “The location and material culture of the temporary occupation at Lacroix Inlet point to a connection between this site and the nearby shipwreck remains and thus, possibly with the Espora and her crew.”

At the camp, which the team described as a “short-term occupation,” they found glass beads, buttons, and a bottle, along with nautical items such as a deck prism and a rudder hinge. Elsewhere in the inlet lay the remains of three wooden hulls, including timber that may have been used to build a structure. All the wood likely came from ships’ hulls, but it’s unclear whether it all came from the same vessel.

The team called the finds “novel data” on the history of seafaring around the island. Their preliminary assessment points to at least one shipwreck that led to a temporary settlement. “The identity of the vessel/s and the castaways’ trajectories are the subject of ongoing inquiry,” they wrote, adding that a thorough study of the timbers may provide definitive answers.

Some artifacts are especially telling. “The deck glass located on the surface is one of the most revealing artifacts,” Ciarlo told Discover Magazine. “To assess the identity of the Espora—as it happens with other shipwreck sites—is like putting together a puzzle. It does not rely on a unique proof, but on a critical analysis and merging of multiple lines of evidence.”

Still, questions remain. In the study, the authors acknowledged that they found no trace of the site where the Luisito was built, and it’s unclear whether the Espora was ever completely taken apart. They wrote that more work is needed at the camp and on the shipwrecks in the weather-beaten inlet.

“As archaeologists,” Ciarlo said, according to Phys.org, “being in this isolated and wild place allowed us to taste what a small group of castaways saw and felt about 150 years ago.”

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6347. This Bissell Carpet Cleaner Is Lightweight, Compact, and Easy to Store—All for Under $125

If you live in a smaller space or multilevel home, the TurboClean is worth a look.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Carpet cleaning is one of those chores that feels like a massive undertaking every time—not to mention, no one likes having to lug around a heavy carpet cleaner sloshing with water. The Bissell TurboClean Upright Carpet Cleaner is made for people like us, with a lightweight design and minimal learning curve.

This machine is great for small spaces, and for those who prefer streamlined and simplified household appliances. Although it does have a smaller water tank capacity and lacks handheld attachments, it provides a powerful clean paired with easy maneuverability and fast drying time.

The compact design makes it easy both to use and to store. It’ll be sitting alongside your favorite dry vacuum as a trusted staple of your cleaning routine in no time, as I found to be the case for myself.

I set aside a weekend morning to test the TurboClean upright across a frequently used area of my main living space, spanning the pathway from the door to the garage through to the kitchen. The area includes some carpet that I've vacuumed frequently, but not deep-cleaned in years, as well as a low-pile area rug. I didn’t pretreat the area with dry vacuuming, but I checked for any larger pieces of debris that might clog up the cleaner.

The cleaner was quick and easy to assemble, and filling the water tank was simple too. I followed the manufacturer’s instructions to add some of the included Bissell cleaning solution along with warm water. Afterward, I tackled my designated area of carpeting, followed by a section of the area rug.

Throughout the process, I monitored how well the cleaner performed in a few ways. I kept an eye on how long the water tank lasted before I had to empty the dirty water and refill the clean tank, as well as how many times I had to go over an area for a satisfactory clean. I also maneuvered the machine as close as possible to the baseboards and into corners to test movability and range. Finally, I checked how long it took for the carpet to dry afterward, as well as how easy it was to clean the machine when I wrapped it all up.

The first thing I noticed about the TurboClean Upright was its lightness. Weighing just under 13 pounds, it’s one of the lightest carpet cleaners I’ve tried. That light weight, combined with a compact base and smooth wheels, made it especially easy to move around, whether I was pulling it along straight pathways, turning corners, or navigating as close to the wall as I could get. Even with a full tank, I found it very manageable.

That lightness, though, didn’t mean flimsiness or poor performance. On the contrary: it pulled up considerably more dirt than I expected, providing a deep, visible clean on a high-traffic area of light-colored carpet.

While I didn’t have any serious stains for it to handle, it did do a great job on visible spots of dirt or water-drop stains that had become dried-in. It worked equally well on the area rug, refreshing it without damaging the fibers or dulling the colors.

As a compact machine, the TurboClean Upright does have one of the hallmark downsides to its class: the need for frequent refills. The water tank has a capacity of just over half a gallon. As I worked through my test area, I had to stop, empty the dirty water tank, and refill the cleaner with fresh water and cleaning solution.

If you’re trying to spot-clean a few small patches, you can probably get away without a refill, but if you’re actually doing a whole room or more, you’ll need to do the empty-and-refill routine—probably multiple times. It’s also worth noting that the machine does not heat the water from within. It recommends adding warm water (no warmer than 140°F) to the clean tank with the solution.

Fortunately, the process of refilling and, later, disassembling and cleaning, is very easy. The tank and handle feel a little light to the touch, but they’re sturdier than they seem, and it’s easy to get a grip and handle the empty/refill cycle without making a mess. Disassembling the main parts (the upper tank and the two-part handle) is as easy as the push of a button. There’s really very little in the way of maintenance, which I appreciated.

If you plan on cleaning an area with a lot of debris (like pet hair), I would suggest vacuuming first. Otherwise, you do run the risk of particles getting tangled up around the cleaning brush, which can take a while to get cleared.

For me, the biggest downside to this cleaner is its lack of any hand tools. Where most home carpet cleaners come with at least a handheld tool or a spot-cleaning tool of some kind, the basic model TurboClean Upright has none. While it’s still a light and small enough machine to maneuver around most spaces, the lack of extensions and tools does limit what it can do.

I was able to lower it enough to clean underneath a coffee table, and I could get fairly close to the wall, but not quite as deep into the corners. I wish there had been a stain tool, a pet tool, or even just a simple hand tool extension. Without those, the cleaner is unable to handle smaller crevices or upholstery.

I didn’t have any deep, dark stains that needed removing, but if I did have those, it would have been nice to be able to really focus the cleaning power on those areas. As currently designed, the best I could do was simply run the full cleaner over the same spot repeatedly.

All that being said, the TurboClean Upright does come in a deluxe “Pet” model as well. That model does include a 7-foot extendible hose, a self-cleaning “tough stains” brush, and a spraying crevice tool. Those additions offer more flexibility to tackle small spots and get into crevices, improving the cleaner’s performance and versatility. And, of course, anyone with pets will definitely want to look into this upgrade to gain the extra cleaning power for pet stains and hair.

The TurboClean Upright comes with two trial-size Bissell cleaning formulas: the Pro Max Clean + Protect and the Pet Pro Oxy Urine Eliminator. I used the Pro Max solution for deep cleaning, adding it to the clean tank up to the indicated “formula” line. The instructions also indicate that users can add a dose of the “Oxy Boost” formula for a stronger cleaning reaction, but since I didn’t have that on hand, I skipped that step.

After multiple passes across my testing area, I really appreciated the strong suction power. Although there’s not a specific “quick dry” mode, the manual does suggest running “dry passes” across the wet areas to suction up as much of the residual water as possible. It only took between one and two hours for the test section to feel pretty much dry to the touch.

The Bissell TurboClean Upright is ideal for smaller spaces and intuitive operation, bringing plenty of cleaning power but keeping the machine itself relatively compact and lightweight. I was able to easily clean carpeting and an area rug, and I could move around corners easily.

The smaller size does mean a smaller tank (requiring more frequent stops to refill), and I wish the standard model included some attachment tools for greater versatility. Still, if you’re looking for a reliable cleaner for a smaller area that does the job well (and doesn’t leave your carpet sopping wet), this could be a great pick for you.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.
