#6345. The 8 Best Salt Spreaders for Getting Out Ahead of Winter Storms

They’re more reliable and durable than a basic fertilizer spreader.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter doesn’t have to be severe for ice to be a problem—even one small storm can leave a slippery layer of frozen water that causes a fall. But putting down a simple layer of snow melt can easily prevent any accidents. It can also reduce the amount of time you have to mess with shovels or snowblowers. But believe it or not, how you put it down matters, and the best salt spreaders are there to guide you.

Snow melt, typically rock salt or calcium chloride, melts existing ice and prevents new ice from forming. Using a salt spreader, which spins and sprays your snow melt all around, helps ensure you get a nice, even coat over any area you prep. Gardeners may recognize the salt spreader as a close cousin of the fertilizer spreader, but with a more robust construction to endure winter weather and the corrosive nature of salt.

Salt spreaders come in a wide array of sizes to suit different jobs, including small handheld spreaders for front stoops and short walkways, walk-behind models for a long driveway, and large tow-behind spreaders for prepping parking lots. Whether you need to de-ice a front walk or an entire parking lot, we can help you find the best salt spreader for your snow removal situation.

Tony Carrick tapped his experience covering landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security to find the salt spreaders worth the money. Reviews Editor David Dritsas—who covers landscaping, tools, and DIY, including outdoor tools like snow blowers and snow shovels—then updated these recommendations ahead of winter. They picked the best salt spreaders based on their experiences using various models to treat driveways and sidewalks around the home. They also researched industry standards, detailed specifications, and user recommendations from customer reviews.

This salt spreader’s size, ability to control salt flow, and reasonable price tag make it a great all-around choice for salt spreading. With its 80-pound capacity, it can cover the average driveway, as well as sidewalks and walkways in a single load. It also comes well equipped to handle winter weather with large, pneumatic 12-inch wheels and a sturdy steel frame.

The spreader features a plastic spiked auger (though we prefer a metal spiked auger) that cuts through clumps of most deicing salts, preventing clogs. You should, however, avoid using rock salt, as it is larger and could get caught in the plastic construction.

We appreciate its three adjustable baffles, which allow you to reduce or expand its coverage area to prevent overspread onto the lawn and landscaping. This is a great mid-size salt spreader and a perfect fit for most homes.

If you’re looking to get the most bang for your buck out of a spreader, then go with this model from Scotts. Not only can you spread salt with it, but you can also use it to seed and fertilize your lawn. Unlike most fertilizer spreaders, this model can spread ice melt. Additionally, it features rubber tires, unlike the plastic wheels found on other Scotts spreaders, allowing it to handle icy conditions.

There’s a dial that gives you precise control over how much salt, seed, or fertilizer you’re releasing with each step—this is common on fertilizer spreaders but not so much with salt spreaders. And since it has Scott’s EdgeGuard technology, you can treat walks and driveways without showering your grass and landscaping with salt.

This combination of features makes it a great jack-of-all-trades spreader for those who want one machine for all seasons.

This top-of-the-line spreader from EarthWay can handle large jobs, holding up to 100 pounds, with holes and an auger large enough to pass rock salt up to 3 inches in size, plus a very large, 15-foot spread width.

It’s a little bit heavier than other models on our list—30 pounds alone before you even add the salt—but it rolls on two large, knobby 13-inch pneumatic tires, which help you avoid slipping and sliding over icy terrain.

These features make this walk-behind model a good option for professionals or homeowners with large paved areas to prep.

There’s no sense investing in an expensive walk-behind salt spreader if you only have to clear a walkway or front stoop. This handheld model gets the job done and doesn’t cost much. Plus, you can use it in the warmer months to seed and fertilize small patches of lawn and landscaping beds.

There are separate spreader settings for seed, fertilizer, and ice melt, and it holds up to 2 pounds of product. It even has an ergonomic arm support that makes it relatively comfortable to hold while you’re spreading product. Sure, it would be easier to use if it were automatic, but we’ll take the low-cost manual option any day of the week.

If you only need a small spreader but don’t want to deal with a hand crank, this rechargeable electric model may work better for you. It runs on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, and in addition to working with salt and de-icer, you can also use it for seeds and fertilizer.

It has eight flow rate settings, allowing you to release as little or as much as you like, though levels 7 and 8 are intended for use with heavy salts. The speed is variable, and you can adjust the spread up to 127 degrees with a lever on the side. Narrowing the spread can help you be more precise and protect garden beds or lawns from getting salt burn.

The hopper is 2.7 liters, and the battery runs for up to two hours, making this motorized spreader more than up to the challenge of covering the driveways and sidewalks of most average homes. Since it's battery-powered and listed as not waterproof, it's recommended to clean it of any moisture when you're done using it.

Agri-Fab’s massive salt spreader offers one of the largest capacities of any non-professional-grade walk-behind model we’ve seen. Its massive hopper can hold a whopping 130 pounds of salt, which is enough to cover a long service road or an 80-car parking lot. It’s built to handle all that weight with a frame made from 1-inch-thick steel tubing. The large 12-inch pneumatic tires have heavy treads to prevent slipping on snow and ice.

The heavy-duty design wouldn’t be complete without a stainless steel impeller to break up clogs. It also features a waterproof cover to keep the ice melt dry if you have to go out on a rainy day. This commercial-grade salt spreader is built for big jobs.

If you’ve got an ATV or lawn tractor and a lot of ground to cover, spare your back and mount this towable spreader. With its 185-pound capacity, a single load can cover up to an acre of soon-to-be-snowy ground.

The universal hitch will work with all tractors, UTVs, and ATVs. The control rod extends far enough that you won’t have to get out of the driver’s seat to adjust the flow of salt. Its 15-inch pneumatic tires and thick-gauge steel frame keep it stable, even when pulled a little too fast. There’s also a hopper cover that keeps the salt from getting wet while working in rain or snow.

This is a great option if you have a long driveway or a large parking area to cover.

Due to its mountable design, this salt spreader gives you the capacity of a towable spreader, but won’t compromise the maneuverability of a four-wheeler. This semipro spreader can hold up to 15 gallons of ice melt, which means it’s really made for prepping long service roads, parking lots, and commercial spaces, rather than homes.

The ATVS15A spreader uses a plate and auger powered by a 23-volt motor to launch a 30-foot-wide swath of salt. The hopper has a lid that keeps your ice melt dry and prevents it from bouncing out of the top of the hopper.

Since you sit right in front of the spreader, accessing the on/off switch and gate controls is convenient from the driver’s seat. This is a solid commercial option for contractors who need to prep worksites, workers in small communities with service roads, and commercial areas that might be easier to reach on an ATV than a truck.

These are compact, watering can-sized basins with a handle and either a hand crank or a motorized trigger mechanism. Their compact size and light weight make spreading salt easy work, provided you only need to cover a small area. They can’t hold much salt and have a limited range, so they’re best reserved for small jobs like patio doorways, stoops, or a short front walkway.

This type of spreader sits on two wheels, with a large plastic basin and a spinning impeller at the base. As you push the spreader forward, the salt shoots out the front and both sides of the basin. These wheelbarrow-esque spreaders can hold a large amount of ice melt, so they’re the way to go for most homes with large patios, parking spaces, driveways, and sidewalks.

This is one of the largest options. If you’re responsible for clearing snow off a parking lot or a long driveway that’s more than a couple of hundred feet long, you may want to get a truly massive salt spreader that hitches to the back of an ATV or riding lawn mower.

Some spreaders offer even larger capacities that attach to the trailer hitch on a pickup truck or mount to the back of an ATV. Obviously, these spreaders can hold a much larger amount of salt than a walk-behind. It’s overkill for most homes, but small businesses or farms could use one to prep large parking lots, loading docks, and other large paved areas.

The more ice melt your salt spreader can hold, the more ground you can cover before you need to stop for a refill. As a rule of thumb, you’ll need to spread about 3 pounds of snow melt for every 1,000 square feet of area. Though there is some variation from model to model, picking the right type of spreader is the first and most important step.

Most handheld spreaders only hold enough salt to de-ice a short walk and a front stoop; walk-behind spreaders can hold about 65 to 130 pounds of ice; and towable spreaders often hold up to 185 pounds of salt.

Spread width measures how far your spreader will throw salt as you use it. Most spreaders have a range between 6 feet for walk-behind models and as far as 30 feet for larger towable spreaders.

While a wide spread can save you time, keep in mind that it may also lead you to spray salt onto your lawn and landscaping. Salt will dry out plants, so you want to avoid spraying green areas as much as possible. If you need to salt sidewalks and driveways that border grass and landscaped areas, look for adjustable spreaders with baffles so you can narrow your spread and avoid overspray.

You have a few options when it comes to ice melt. Calcium chloride is the best option. It melts ice even at extreme sub-zero temperatures, won’t harm your plants, and is less toxic than rock salt, but it’s also pricier.

Rock salt is the cheapest, but‌ it’s more toxic, won’t work in extreme cold, and can clog spreaders more easily. Magnesium chloride is the least toxic option and works at temperatures as low as 5 degrees Fahrenheit.

Whichever ice melt you choose, be sure to use it as directed, as all of the above can eat away at wood, steel, and concrete.

While they operate similarly, we don’t recommend putting rock salt in a fertilizer/seed spreader. Dedicated salt spreaders store corrosive salt and endure icy winter conditions. Using a fertilizer spreader to spread salt once or twice won’t break it, but it won’t work as well and may shorten its lifespan in the long term.

Salt spreaders typically have hoppers made from thick, durable plastic that sit on heavy-gauge steel frames and feature pneumatic rubber wheels with heavy tread that can grip slick paved surfaces. They also come equipped with metal moving parts that are capable of chopping up hard salt without wearing down.

If you want one spreader to do double duty, it would probably make more sense to use a salt spreader to spread seed or fertilizer. That said, fertilizer/seed spreaders often provide more precise control of the spread direction and quantity, which comes in handy when you have specific patches to cover and you want to be precise. Keep in mind that adding too much fertilizer to a lawn can cause it to burn out.

If you do put fertilizer in your salt spreader (or vice versa), make sure to clean out the salt thoroughly before placing any seed or fertilizer in the hopper. Any lingering salt in the mix will dry out the grass, damaging your lawn.

Bottom line: We would recommend buying two separate spreaders, despite their similarities.

Most residential-use salt spreaders can't handle rock salt, while many professional-level salt spreaders can. Check with the manufacturer to determine what types of de-icer are compatible with your salt spreader before loading it with rock salt, as it can damage the spreader’s impeller.

If rock salt isn’t compatible with your spreader, use a different type of ice melt, such as potassium chloride, magnesium chloride, or calcium chloride.

#6344. Billions of trees grow beyond forests – and counting them could change restoration plans

A satellite study counted 5.25 billion trees in Rwanda and Tanzania, finding more than half outside forests, from farmland to towns.

Count a country’s forests and you’ve counted its trees, or so the thinking goes. In Rwanda and Tanzania, most of the trees aren’t in the forests at all.

Researchers counted about 5.25 billion trees across the two countries from 2019 satellite images, and more than half stood on farms, in grassland and shrubland, and in towns.

Countries and organizations have pledged to plant more than a trillion trees worldwide since the Paris climate agreement of 2015.

A pledge needs a count of what is already there, and that count has mostly come from forest surveys that often exclude farmland.

Maurice Mugabowindekwe and Martin Brandt of the University of Copenhagen led the team, with colleagues at the Rwanda Space Agency, the University of Rwanda, and the Tanzania Forest Services Agency.

Their count covers only trees big enough to see from space. That means a crown of at least 32 square feet (3 square meters), or a height of at least 10 feet (3 meters).

The team sorted its count by the land cover map that the European Space Agency’s WorldCover project publishes.

Only 48.8% of the trees fell inside the class that map calls tree cover, which is roughly forest and woodland.

The other 51.2% were spread across everything else: shrubland held 22.1%, grassland 16.4%, and cropland 12%.

The rest, under 1%, stood in towns, wetlands, bare ground and mangroves. Counting only trees in the tree-cover category would leave out more than half the total.

Tanzania accounted for about 5.04 billion of the trees and Rwanda for about 213 million. The typical acre in Tanzania carried 17 trees (42 per hectare) and the typical acre in Rwanda 15 (37 per hectare).

A typical acre of forest carried about 25 (61 per hectare). Forest holds trees more thickly, but there is far more land outside it.

In 2015, a team writing in Nature estimated about 19.9 billion trees in Tanzania, nearly four times this count.

The estimates are not directly comparable: the earlier study included small trees beneath the canopy, while the new study also counted trees outside forests.

Older tree maps worked from pictures sharp enough to outline each crown, taken by drones, aircraft or satellites. Those images cost money, and clouds spoil many.

The Planet satellites the team used have a 10-foot (3-meter) pixel.

The freely available Sentinel-2 optical images and Sentinel-1 radar data have 33-foot (10-meter) pixels.

So the team stopped trying to outline crowns. They stacked 20 bands of data from the three satellite systems into one image and cut it into squares 315 feet (96 meters) on a side.

Then they trained a deep learning model to estimate how many trees each square held, from the patterns of color, texture and radar echo inside it.

The model learned from about 12 million tree crowns in 2,832 sample areas across nine African countries and India. People had marked those crowns by hand or pulled them from laser-scanner height maps.

The team also found that dropping the sharper Planet images and using only the two Sentinel satellites gave nearly the same accuracy.

Rwanda and Tanzania both run national forest inventories, in which crews measure the trees in fixed plots.

The team compared its predictions with 196 of those plots in Rwanda and 19,664 in Tanzania.

It counted only trees at least 8 inches (20 centimeters) thick at chest height, the size most likely to show from above.

The model undercounted in most landscapes. Its raw estimate was about 179 million trees for Rwanda and 3.79 billion for Tanzania.

Matching the field plots raised those figures by about a fifth and a third, respectively, to the 213 million and 5.04 billion reported.

The authors’ explanation is that overlapping crowns in dense forest blur into one signal at a 10-foot pixel.

Built-up areas and mangroves in Tanzania were overcounted instead, and the authors suspect buildings and wetland plants were being read as trees.

Even after correction, the Tanzania figure could be anywhere from 4.6 to 5.6 billion.

A survey of East African farms found an average of 79 trees per acre (195 per hectare).

At that density, the two countries’ 37.6 million acres (15.2 million hectares) of cropland could take about 2.3 billion more trees.

That would be nearly half as many again as the two countries hold now, and trees among crops can raise harvests as well, the authors added.

Tanzania’s own census counts far more cropland than the satellite map does, about 99 million acres (40 million hectares), half of it on smallholder farms.

On that figure, the authors wrote, smallholders alone could add around 3.4 billion trees “if they access adequate support and incentives.”

That is more trees than the count found in all of Tanzania’s forests.

The authors’ point is that a baseline like this one can guide where a government puts its restoration money, and where planting new trees would crowd out naturally open land.

Restoration programs across Africa, from national pledges to the Great Green Wall, have mostly had no such baseline, because operational tree-count systems remain largely unavailable, the authors wrote.

The satellites can’t see under a dense canopy, so the authors treat their own estimates for closed forest with caution.

The count also leaves out every tree too small to show at a 10-foot pixel, so it can’t yet tell whether newly planted seedlings survive.

The correction factors came from Rwandan and Tanzanian field plots, so they may not apply elsewhere.

To use this method elsewhere, researchers would need local field measurements to check and adjust the satellite estimates.

The data and code are publicly available. The team plans to incorporate field measurements into the model to better account for trees hidden beneath the canopy.

The researchers also hope to test the method in other regions and with data from other satellites.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Remote Sensing.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.
